## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Tatiyanānātitthiya Sutta* (Ud 6.6) is the third discourse in the *Udāna* dealing with the controversies of non-Buddhist sectarians [DharmaNexus]. In this sutta, wanderers of various outside schools fall into heated disputation concerning the nature of the self (*attā*), the world (*loko*), pleasure, and pain [Levman 2014]. In particular, they debate whether the self and the world are created by oneself or by another (*sayamkato ca paramkato ca attā ca loko ca*) [Levman 2014]. The Buddha encapsulates the futility of these sectarian views in an inspired utterance (*udāna* / *gāthā*), observing that people are bound by the notions that "I am the doer" (*ahaṅkāra*) or that "another is the doer" (*paraṅkāra*) [Levman 2014].

The discourse shares extensive textual formulaic material with its immediate predecessors, the *Paṭhamanānātitthiya Sutta* (Ud 6.4) and *Dutiyanānātitthiya Sutta* (Ud 6.5), as well as significant doctrinal phrases with other early discourses including the *Pāsādika Sutta* (DN 29), the *Pañcattaya Sutta* (MN 102), and the *Apaṇṇaka Sutta* (MN 60) [DharmaNexus]. Verse parallels to the closing *udāna* are preserved in chapter 27 (*Paśyavarga* / *Sight*) across multiple recensions and translations of the *Udānavarga*, including the Sanskrit text, Tibetan translations, and Chinese versions (T 212 and T 213) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also detects cross-linguistic textual alignments with the Chinese *Dīrghāgama* (T 1) and the Tibetan translation of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* [DharmaNexus].
